These numbers describe Louisville as a whole, so a given street can sit well above or below them.

Lexington by the numbers

Does the city of Lexington send its own property tax bill?

No separate city bill exists, because Lexington and Fayette County operate as one government. The Lexington-Fayette Urban County Government (LFUCG) replaced the separate city and county governments in the early 1970s, when police and fire services were merged, and the Fayette County Sheriff collects property tax for the whole territory. The Fayette County PVA, which values every parcel, says on its rate page that the total bill is built from rates set by the Commonwealth, the LFUCG, Fayette County Public Schools and a few other districts.

What differs from one Lexington address to the next is the service district. Seven residential districts appear on the PVA's 2026 chart, and each pays the same base lines for state, schools, general services, the extension office, soil conservation, public health, Lextran buses and parks. Only the curbside extras separate them.

  • The full-service district adds 17.3 cents per $100 for trash pickup, street lights and street cleaning.
  • Districts with only refuse add 13.7 cents, only street lights 2.7 cents, and combinations fall in between.
  • The school line is the biggest piece of every bill at 79.7 cents per $100, about 63 percent of the full-service total of $1.2598.

On a home assessed at $300,000, the gap between the full-service district and the district without optional services is $519 a year. Find the district number on your bill or ask the PVA, because it changes what a buyer will pay each month.

How do blighted-property and downtown charges change a Lexington bill?

Two surcharges apply only in certain places. When the LFUCG Vacant Property Review Commission labels a parcel abandoned and blighted, the owner pays $1 more per $100 of taxable value. On a $200,000 assessment, that is $2,000 a year on top of the normal bill, which makes a neglected vacant house expensive to hold. A parcel inside the Downtown Lexington Management District pays an extra 10 cents per $100.

Owners of empty houses should learn whether the commission has certified theirs before listing. The LFUCG can tell you, and a buyer will price the surcharge into any offer.

Why does Lexington's Urban Service Area matter to a seller?

In 1958 Lexington became the first American city to adopt an urban growth boundary. Inside it, in the urban service area, development could proceed at city density. Outside, in the rural service area, parcels had to be at least 40 acres, a rule meant to shield the horse farms around town. A 1980 plan update added urban and rural activity centers, the rural ones clustered around the I-64 and I-75 interchanges. The boundary was widened in 1996 by 5,300 acres, and in 2000 the city adopted a purchase-of-development-rights program that received $40 million in 2001, made of $25 million from local sources and $15 million from the state.

For a seller, the line decides which kind of parcel you have. Property outside it can sit on a large lot in farm use, and Kentucky assesses farmland at agricultural value instead of market value, which changes the tax math completely. Pull the parcel record from the PVA to confirm the tax district and land use before pricing. Expect different answers for a subdivision lot inside the line and for acreage outside it.

How big has Lexington grown?

The consolidated city spans 285.5 square miles, almost all of it land. Its metro area reaches into Clark, Jessamine, Bourbon, Woodford and Scott counties, held 516,811 people in 2020, and ranks second in Kentucky behind Louisville. Adding Richmond and Frankfort gives a combined area of 747,919. A party of frontiersmen under William McConnell camped at the site in June 1775 and named it for Lexington, Massachusetts, after hearing of the fighting there. Forty-five settlers signed the Lexington Compact on January 25, 1780.

The jump from 108,137 to 204,165 across the 1970s came in the same decade that the city and county governments merged. Since 1990 each decade has added between 9 and 16 percent.

What should I know about Lexington's schools, roads and weather before listing?

The Lexington entry on Wikipedia describes a Fayette County Public Schools system of six district high schools, 12 middle schools and 37 elementary schools, with many private schools on top of that. The University of Kentucky and Transylvania University are the two traditional colleges, and Blue Grass Airport is on the west side along US 60. I-75 skirts the city and I-64 runs along the north. US 25, 27, 60, 68 and 421 meet in Lexington, which has few freeways and a reputation for congestion.

Weather is moderate and fairly wet. A typical year brings about 49.8 inches of precipitation, 14.5 inches of snow, 25 days of 90-degree heat and 23 winter days that stay below freezing. The Asthma and Allergy Foundation of America also rates the area as high-allergy.

What happens to unpaid Lexington property tax?

Once a bill is delinquent, the Fayette County Clerk is the office to deal with, and its rules are rigid. A delinquent bill is a lien, so the clerk wants certified funds. Interest raises the balance each month.

  • Accepted: cash, a money order, or a cashier's or certified check payable to the Fayette County Clerk.
  • Turned away: personal checks, business checks, counter checks and credit cards.
  • Not available: partial payments on a delinquent bill.

Owners who cannot pay in full can phone the Fayette County Attorney's Office at 859-254-4941 to ask about a payment arrangement.

Visit Room 132 at 162 E. Main Street, Lexington, KY 40507, or call 859-253-3344 during payoff hours of 8:00 to 4:30. The clerk's deeds website has a search tool and a calculator. Every year the clerk sells eligible delinquent bills to third-party purchasers between 90 and 135 days after the sheriff's handoff. The 2026 sale was held July 24 at 11:00 a.m., and registration details for 2027 are due in spring 2027. A seller should obtain the payoff before the listing goes live.

What do Lexington sellers owe when the deed is recorded?

Selling a house here triggers the state transfer tax in KRS 142.050: $0.50 for each $500 of price, with any leftover fraction counted as a full unit. A $325,000 sale produces $325. The grantor bears it, and the Fayette County Clerk computes it and collects before the deed can be filed. Foreclosure transfers, transfers between spouses in a divorce, and parent-to-child transfers for nominal consideration are exempt.

Property tax runs on a separate track. Whoever held title at the start of the year gets the bill, and the contract or settlement statement says how the cost is divided. A seller who is 65 or disabled may be receiving the $49,100 homestead exemption in force for 2025 and 2026, but a buyer must file a new application with the Fayette County PVA.

More questions about Lexington, KY Property Tax Guide

Is there a separate city property tax in Lexington?

No. Lexington and Fayette County share one urban county government, so the single bill from the Fayette County Sheriff covers state, school, county and urban-government charges. Rates depend on the service district of your address.

What is the biggest part of a Lexington tax bill?

The school line. On the PVA's 2026 chart it is 79.7 cents per $100 in each residential district, set against a full-service total of $1.2598.

How much extra does a blighted Lexington property pay?

An extra $1 per $100 of taxable value once the LFUCG Vacant Property Review Commission certifies it as abandoned and blighted. On a $200,000 assessment that is $2,000 a year.

Can I pay delinquent Lexington tax with a credit card?

No. The Fayette County Clerk takes only cash, money orders and cashier's or certified checks for delinquent bills, and it does not accept partial payments.

What is the Lexington transfer tax on a home sale?

Under KRS 142.050 the seller pays $0.50 per $500 of price at recording, so a $325,000 sale carries a $325 charge, collected by the Fayette County Clerk.
